About: Euclidean Distance as a Scalar Invariant

Source

Lecture
4 — Scalar invariants
Simulation
Simulation 2 — the Euclidean space & metric demo from Lecture 2, extended with controls that translate the origin and rotate the axes (guided-inquiry mode).
Concept
The Euclidean distance between two points is a scalar invariant — unchanged by translations or rotations of the coordinate system, even though each point's coordinates change.
Serves
Identify translations & rotations as coordinate transformations; use the Euclidean metric to define invariants; distinguish scalars from vectors; derive the spatial distance (interval) as a scalar invariant; treat invariance as the guide for constructing physical observables.
Inquiry
Are Δx, Δy invariant under translation? Under rotation? What combination of them is invariant under both — and why?
Misconception
"If the coordinates change, the distance computed from them must change too." (Encoded as prediction choices a/b; rebutted only on selection.)
Kick-off
Students formulate their own definition of "physical observable" from the simulation evidence before the formal one is given (Claudia's prompt).

Guided Inquiry

1 · Two points on a plane

Let’s set things up. Points A and B sit at fixed places on a plane, and a Cartesian coordinate system is laid over them. Its origin can be shifted by (Tx, Ty), and its axes can be turned through an angle θ.

Keep in mind that every number on screen — each point’s coordinates, the differences Δx′ and Δy′, and the distance d — is read in whichever coordinate system you’re currently using.

2 · Shifting the origin

First, we’ll slide the grid. The origin of the coordinate system is moved while A and B stay exactly where they are. Which quantities do you think change?

3 · Turning the axes

Now for a twist. The origin stays put and the axes are turned through θ instead. What do you think happens to the distance d?

4 · Both at once

Next, combine both moves. The origin is shifted and the axes are turned together. Which quantities do you think read the same as they did in the original coordinate system?

5 · When is d zero?

One last experiment. Bring A and B together until they very nearly coincide, then separate them again. Which statement about d do you think is true?

6 · The Euclidean metric

Let’s bring it all together. The rule d² = Δx′² + Δy′² is the Euclidean metric: it turns coordinate differences into a length. Two properties make it the right rule — it’s invariant under any shift of the origin or turn of the axes, and it’s positive-definite, vanishing only for coincident points.

The Physics

Euclidean space and the metric · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

Two points sit fixed on a plane, and you choose the coordinate axes that describe them. This sim lets you shift and turn those axes and compare the numbers you read in each choice, the idea that relativity later applies to space and time.

What you'll learn

  • How the sim turns A and B into coordinates in shifted and turned axes.
  • How the coordinates, the differences Δx′ and Δy′, and the distance d each respond to a shift of the origin and to a turn of the axes.
  • How the Euclidean metric combines two differences into one length.
  • What it means for a quantity to be a scalar, and why physics is written with scalars.
A and B stay fixed. Dashed grey: the original axes. Solid: the axes you turn.

What's on screen

  • A (cyan dot): the first point. Drag it anywhere on the plane.
  • B (amber dot): the second point, also draggable.
  • White line: the straight line from A to B. Its length is d.
  • Grey axes with unit ticks and an origin: the coordinate system. They read x, y, O until you move them, then x′, y′, O′.
  • Dashed legs: Δx′ (green) along x′, then Δy′ (pink) along y′, ending at B.
  • Readouts (top right): the coordinates of A and B, Δx′, Δy′ and d, in the current axes.
See itLet the axes turn by themselves, with A and B at their opening places. Watch for: the grid and axes turning around A and B, which do not move.

03

The sim moves the axes, not the points

A and B have fixed positions on the plane. You control the coordinate system that describes them: Tx and Ty put its origin at (Tx, Ty), and θ turns both axes anticlockwise. Moving the axes while the points stay put is called a passive transformation.

The sim's map from the original coordinates (x, y) to the new ones (x′, y′): shift the origin, then turn the axes.

Every number on screen is read in the current axes, which is why the sim adds primes once you move them. The two differences are Δx′ = x′B − x′A and Δy′ = y′B − y′A. They are the legs of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is the line AB, and d is the length of that line.

See itPut the origin at (2, 1) and turn the axes through 30°. Watch for: the origin O′ and the axes moving to their new places while A and B stay where they were.
04

A shift of the origin cancels in every difference

Moving the origin changes both points' coordinates by the same amount, Tx in x and Ty in y. Subtracting one point from the other removes that common amount:

Δx′ = (xB − Tx) − (xA − Tx) = xB − xA = Δx, and likewise Δy′ = Δy.

  • The coordinates change. With Tx = 3 and Ty = −2 the default points A = (−1, −1) and B = (2, 3) read A′ = (−4, 1) and B′ = (−1, 5).
  • The differences do not. They stay Δx′ = 3 and Δy′ = 4. A coordinate says where a point is relative to the origin you chose. A difference compares the two points, so it never refers to the origin.
  • The distance d is built from these differences (section 06), so a shift leaves it unchanged too.
See itPut the origin at (3, −2) with the axes unturned. Watch for: the coordinates of A and B changing while Δx′ stays 3.00 and Δy′ stays 4.00.
05

A turn changes the legs but not the sum of their squares

Once the shift has cancelled, only θ is left. A turn mixes the original differences Δx and Δy:

The differences in the turned axes. Tx and Ty do not appear.

At θ = 30° the default legs 3 and 4 become 4.60 and 1.96. Add the squares and the cross terms cancel, leaving cos²θ + sin²θ = 1:

The sum of squares is the same in every turned set of axes.
Tx Ty θ

These sliders move the sim too. After dragging A or B, reopen the sheet to update.

The line above recomputes d from the legs in your current axes. The sim's own d readout is computed from the points' original coordinates.

See itLet the axes turn through a full circle. Watch for: Δx′ and Δy′ changing continuously while d stays at 5.00.
06

The metric turns two differences into one length

The rule d² = Δx′² + Δy′² is the Euclidean metric δij: Pythagoras' theorem, applied to the components in whatever Cartesian axes you use.

The metric combines two components into one length.
  • d is never negative. It is the square root of a sum of squares, and it is 0 only when Δx′ = Δy′ = 0, that is, when A and B are the same point.
  • Δx′ and Δy′ are components of one vector, the step from A to B, so they depend on the axes. d is a scalar: a single number that every choice of Cartesian axes agrees on. For the default points, d = √(3² + 4²) = 5.
See itPut B on top of A. Watch for: Δx′, Δy′ and d all reading 0.00.
07

Where it matters

Lecture 4's example: one velocity, written in two sets of axes that differ by 45°.
  • Speed is a scalar too. One particle has V = (v/√2)(1, 1) in Bob's axes and Ṽ = (v, 0) in Alice's. The components differ, but V₁² + V₂² = v² in both.
  • Mapping and surveying. Two survey teams that set up different axes record different coordinates for the same two landmarks. In the same units, over a patch small enough to treat as flat, they agree on the distance between them.
  • Spacetime. Lecture 5 keeps this recipe and changes the metric. In this course's convention the interval is ΔS² = Δx² + Δy² + Δz² − c²Δt², with c the speed of light, and every inertial observer agrees on it. ΔS² < 0 is timelike, = 0 lightlike, > 0 spacelike.
Go deeper: the recipe belongs to Cartesian axes

δij survives shifts, turns and reflections of Cartesian axes. It does not survive every change of coordinates. Take the points (1, 0) and (0, 1), whose true distance has d² = 2. Written in polar coordinates (r, φ) they are (1, 0°) and (1, 90°), and adding the squared polar differences gives Δr² + Δφ² = 0 + (π/2)² ≈ 2.47. Polar components need a different metric.

08

Summary

In one line. A shift of the origin leaves Δx′ and Δy′ alone, a turn mixes them, and d = √(Δx′² + Δy′²) comes out the same in every Cartesian choice of axes.

Key points

  • A shift changes the coordinates but not the differences.
  • A turn changes Δx′ and Δy′, but cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 keeps their sum of squares.
  • d is a scalar. It is never negative, and it is 0 only when A and B coincide.

Common mix-ups

  • "The coordinates changed, so the distance must have changed." The length of AB does not depend on which axes you read it in.
  • "Δx and Δy are invariant." Only under a shift of the origin. A turn mixes them.
  • "Turning the axes turns the points." Nothing on the plane moves. The axes turn and A and B stay where they were.

Things to try on your own

  • With the default points, set Tx = 3 and Ty = −2, then check A′ and B′ against x′ = x − Tx and y′ = y − Ty.
  • Set θ to 53° and read Δx′ and Δy′. The x′ axis now lies almost along AB. Δx′ is close to d and Δy′ is close to 0.
  • Drag A toward B and watch Δx′, Δy′ and d shrink together.
